figures.caption: Figure 1. Single-unit analysis: from spikes to coding dynamics. (A) Extracellular recordings are high-pass filtered, candidate spikes are detected, and waveform features are clustered to assign events to putative single units. Clustering can be performed in a linear or nonlinear reduced-dimensionality space, such as PC1–PC2 or a UMAP embedding. (B) Recorded activity can be organized as a high-dimensional tensor with axes corresponding to neurons (N), time (t), and conditions (c). (C) Temporal pattern discrimination task (TPDT): the animal reports whether the temporal structure of the second stimulus (P2) matches that of the first stimulus (P1), yielding four condition classes: G–G, G–E, E–G, and E–E (G, grouped; E, extended patterns). Each stimulus lasts 1 s and is followed by a 2-s delay; pd, probe down; kd, key down; pu, probe up; ku, key up; pb, push button. (D) Three example dorsal premotor cortex (DPC) neurons (a–c), with firing rates averaged by class, illustrate the diversity of single-unit coding. (E) Percentage of DPC neurons with significant coding of P1 pattern (cyan), P2 pattern (green), class (pink), partial decision (orange), and complete decision (black) as a function of time; P1 coding persists until mid-P2, when class coding emerges and contributes to the decision signal. Adapted from Rossi-Pool et al. (2016) and Suárez-Barrera et al. (2025).

Figure 2. Low-dimensional population dynamics during parametric working memory. (A) Vibrotactile frequency-discrimination task (Romo et al., 1999): two flutter stimuli (f1, f2) are delivered to the fingertip and separated by a ~3 s delay; the monkey reports whether f1 > f2 (pd/kd, probe/key down; ku, key up; pb, push button). (B) Across-condition correlations of the population state over time, grouped by frequency difference Δf (4–24 Hz): conditions initially converge to a common stimulus-driven state and later separate by Δf, indicating a parametric population code for frequency. Insets show pairwise correlation matrices at selected times. (C) Within-condition cross-correlations referenced to a sensory state and a late-delay memory state: the weak correlation between reference states reveals distinct sensory and mnemonic population representations of the same frequency. (D) Dimensionality-reduction schematic: synthetic firing rates from three example neurons define a population trajectory confined to a low-dimensional plane within neural state space. (E) Leading principal components of prefrontal cortex (PFC) activity during the delay show that a few dimensions capture most firing-rate variance, with the leading component largely reflecting conditionindependent temporal modulation. (F) In the frequency-discrimination task, single neurons show monotonic tuning to stimulus frequency, and the population defines a low-dimensional stimulus subspace, with line-like geometry, in which remembered frequency is stably represented. (G) A similar low-dimensional mnemonic organization arises in an oculomotor delayed-response task, where the stored variable is spatial location and the mnemonic subspace shows a ring-like geometry. Panels B, C adapted from Barak et al. (2010); D, E from Machens et al. (2010); F, G from Murray et al. (2017), with permission of the authors.

Figure 3. Regression axes and demixing of population activity. (A) Context-dependent decision-making task: after fixation and target onset, a random-dot stimulus containing both motion and colour evidence is presented for 0.75 s, followed by a 0.3–1.5 s delay and a saccadic report; a contextual cue instructs the animal to judge either motion or colour while ignoring the other feature. (Bi, Bii) State-space schematics of population trajectories in the motion (Bi) and colour (Bii) contexts, sorted by colour (top) and motion (bottom) evidence: relevant evidence is integrated along the choice axis, whereas irrelevant evidence is represented but not accumulated. (C) Dynamical system implementing the selection vector in the motion (top) and colour (bottom) contexts. Figure 4. Mixed selectivity, orthogonal subspaces, and continuity of single-neuron responses. (A) Example S2 neurons showing firing rates during the two stimulation periods (P1, P2) across TPDT classes G–G, G–E, E–G, and E–E. (B) dPCA projections of S2 activity marginalized with respect to P1. Faithful sensory dynamics are expressed in the first component subspace, whereas transformed categorical dynamics are expressed in a second, nearly orthogonal subspace. (C) Vibrotactile categorization task using two stimulus features, flutter frequency (Hz) and amplitude (mm), each delivered at low or high values across pre-stimulus, stimulus, and delay epochs. Right: dPCA projections showing categorical components (top; frequency modality shown) and a temporal component (bottom), together with their explained variance. Traces are coloured by stimulus frequency level. (D) UMAP embedding of single-neuron response profiles showing heterogeneous but continuous response organization; coloured crosses mark representative functional profiles whose level-dependent trial-averaged responses are shown around the embedding. Panels A, B adapted from Bayones et al. (2024); C, D from Diaz-deLeon et al. (2022).

Figure 5. Flexible temporal processing through cyclic and scaled low-dimensional dynamics. (A) Synchronization–continuation task: the animal taps in synchrony with a periodic stimulus and then continues at the same tempo without external pacing, across target intervals of 450–1000 ms. (B) Population trajectories in the PC2–PC3 plane form cyclic dynamics whose geometry scales with the produced interval. (C) Set–Go interval-production task performed with eye or hand effectors: a cue and a Set pulse define the interval to be reproduced. (D) Example medial frontal cortex neurons showing temporally scaled activity across produced intervals. (E, F) Population trajectories from Set to response scale in time across intervals; the scaling index quantifies the degree of scaling for each component. (G, H) A recurrent network trained to produce the same intervals reproduces the behavioural scaling and provides a mechanistic account: the input sets the initial and terminal fixed points and the speed of evolution between them, whereas recurrent dynamics generate the invariant trajectory. Panels A, B adapted from Gámez et al. (2019), licensed under CC BY 4.0; C–H from Wang et al. (2018).
